title: Spectral theory for dynamical large deviations in non-Markov self-interacting processes
abstract: We develop a spectral theory for dynamical large deviations in non-Markov jump processes and non-Markov chains, whose dynamics depends on the past through state- and jump-dependent empirical observables. We demonstrate that a multiscale Wentzel-Kramers-Brillouin-Jeffreys (WKBJ) Ansatz separates fast configurational relaxation from slow memory evolution, reducing the Feynman--Kac equation for occupation and flux statistics to an eigenvalue problem for a new tilted operator coupled to Hamilton--Jacobi characteristics. This provides a computationally efficient framework for quantifying fluctuations in a broad class of non-Markovian systems. We illustrate our general results with a bistable self-induced East model.
summary: This work establishes a spectral theory for calculating large deviations in complex, non-Markovian systems. By using a WKBJ Ansatz on the Feynman-Kac equation, the authors transform the problem into an eigenvalue problem governed by Hamilton-Jacobi characteristics. This provides a powerful, efficient tool for quantifying rare fluctuations in systems with memory effects, such as self-interacting jump processes.
main_problem: The paper develops a spectral theory to analyze dynamical large deviations in complex, non-Markovian, self-interacting processes.
main_result: The problem is successfully recast as an eigenvalue problem for a tilted operator coupled to Hamilton-Jacobi characteristics, providing a computationally efficient framework for quantifying fluctuations.
method: The authors employ a multiscale Wentzel-Kramers-Brillouin-Jeffreys (WKBJ) Ansatz to solve the Feynman-Kac equation, reducing the dynamics to solving characteristic equations derived from a Hamilton-Jacobi framework.
model_or_system: The theory applies to non-Markov jump processes (SIJPs) and non-Markov chains (SIMCs) whose evolution depends on the system's history via empirical observables (memory). An example used is the bistable self-induced East model.
key_observables: Empirical measure ($L_x$), empirical flux ($\Phi_{xy}$), Scaled Cumulant Generating Function (SCGF), and the rate function $I^*$.
important_parameters: The memory variable $a$ and its conjugate momentum $P$, which govern the slow evolution of the system.
main_assumptions: The method relies on the WKBJ approximation, which separates fast configurational relaxation from slow memory evolution, and assumes the existence of a compact interval $K$ for the memory variable.
figures_summary: Figure 1(a) compares the SCGF of the activity for the self-induced East model at various sizes ($N=6, 8, 10$) against the standard Markov East model.
paper_structure: The paper builds the theory by first deriving the Feynman-Kac equation for the MGF, then applying the WKBJ Ansatz to transform it into an eigenvalue problem. This is subsequently linked to a Hamilton-Jacobi equation, whose characteristics govern the slow memory evolution, culminating in the calculation of the rate function via the SCGF.
why_interesting: The rigorous mathematical machinery developed—linking spectral theory, WKBJ methods, and Hamilton-Jacobi dynamics—is highly relevant for analyzing non-equilibrium dynamics in open quantum systems where memory effects are crucial.

figures.caption: FIG. 1: (a) SCGF of the activity for the self-induced East model at N = 6, 8, 10, compared with the Markov East model at N = 10. In- set: derivative of the SCGF. The increasingly sharp change of slope with N signals an active–inactive dynamical transition, strongly en- hanced by the self-induced feedback. (b) Representative trajectories of the generalised Doob process for ψ = −0.2, 0, 0.2. Negative bias suppresses activity and progressively freezes the dynamics, while positive bias enhances the number of spin flips. The untilted trajec- tory corresponds to typical dynamics of the self-induced East model.
